newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Rice - Vietnam raises rice export quota.
newsitem.headline: Rice - Vietnam raises rice export quota.

text.p: Vietnam, battling a growing trade deficit, has raised its 1996 export quota for rice to three million tonnes, but traders said on Thursday prices for overseas sales were largely unaffected.
An official at the Trade Ministry in Hanoi confirmed local news reports the official quota for this year, previously at 2.5 million tonnes, had been raised.
But dealers said the impact of the move was being offset by rising local prices resulting from transportation and milling delays in southern Vietnam's flood-stricken Mekong Delta.
"It's causing some trouble for rice shipments. The prices in the local market are also going up," said a trader in Ho Chi Minh City.
Five percent broken rice was quoted at around US$275-280 a tonne FOB Saigon Port, with 10 percent grade around $10 per tonne lower. A week ago, five percent broken was trading at about $270 a tonne.
Dealers estimated total rice exports for the first ten months of this year at 2.5 million tonnes. They said 19 vessels were now in Saigon Port, most of them bound for Iran.
Vietnam sold 2.025 million tonnes of rice to overseas buyers in 1995, making it the world's fourth largest rice exporter after the United States, Thailand and India.
This year has seen a bumper crop, partly thanks to earlier harvesting which now takes place ahead of the Mekong Delta flood season.
Thai rice prices firmed this week after monsoon floods prompted the Agriculture Ministry to trim its forecast of Thailand's main crop, trade sources said.

Market sentiment was buoyed by upcoming Japanese rice tenders on Thursday and next month, Syria's planned tender next month, and news that Sri Lanka plans to import more than 500,000 tonnes this year to cover a domestic shortfall.
"There are some good news on demand from Japan and Sri Lanka but whether they will buy from us or not remained to be seen," said another trader.
Syria will tender for 12,000 tonnes for January shipment with results expected on November 20.
Thai 100 percent B benchmark was quoted at about $330-350 a tonne FOB Bangkok against $330-340 last week. Thai 100 percent fragrant rice was quoted at about $615 a tonne against $605 last week.
"Tighter supply pushed prices up. But we haven't heard of any new major orders. Just small orders from regular customers," said a Thai exporter.
"Our prices are higher than those of Vietnam on an average of $30 per tonne...not very attractive," said another trader.
The agriculture ministry this week cut its projection of the 1996/97 (May/January) main paddy (unhusked rice) crop to 17.60 million tonnes from 18.11 million forecast in July.
Some traders discounted the ministry's lower crop forecast, saying the expected flood damage would probably be offset by post-flood replanting.
Ships are loading 55,400 tonnes of rice at river piers near Bangkok this week for Asian, Mideast and African markets.

The loading included 12,000 tonnes of 100 percent grade to Syria, 10,000 tonnes of 100 percent grade to Iran, 13,800 tonnes of 25 percent grade to India, 10,000 tonnes of parboiled rice to Africa, and the rest to unidentified destinations.
The commerce ministry said Thailand exported 4.16 million tonnes of rice during January 1-October 13 against 4.73 million tonnes in the same period a year ago.
In India, rice exporters were negotiating deals for exports to Sri Lanka and Iran as harvesting of the new rice crop started in most rice producing states, traders said.
Mulraj Tanna, a leading Bombay-based foodgrains exporter, said contracts for nearly 120,000 tonnes of rice to Iran and 50,000 tonnes to Sri Lanka were being negotiated.
Prem Garg, a leading Delhi foodgrains exporter, said nearly 200,000 60 kg bags per day of new rice crop had started arriving in the market.
"But the export market is a little bit quiet as Indian rice export prices were still higher compared to Vietnamese prices," Garg said.
Traders said Indian five percent broken non-Basmati rice was currently quoted at $300 per tonne FOB, 10 percent at $280, 15 percent at 255 and 25 percent at $240 per tonne.
"The winter output is expected to be slightly better compared to last year," Tanna said.
